venue.name: Cowichan River Park
venue.description: A provincial park south of Duncan that protects a long stretch of the Cowichan River, a designated BC Heritage River and Canadian Heritage River. BC Parks calls it a recreation corridor, with swimming, canoeing, kayaking, fishing, hiking, cycling and camping. There are four day use areas, at Stoltz Pool, Skutz Falls, Marie Canyon and the 66 Mile Trestle, plus the 20 km Cowichan River Footpath running from Glenora to Skutz Falls and a section of the Trans Canada Trail over two restored railway trestles. This is self guided parkland. BC Parks publishes no interpretive, guided or school program here, only camping and group camping, which schools and non profit youth groups can book at a reduced rate. The park is signposted as Cowichan River Provincial Park and is run for BC Parks by K2 Cowichan Park Services Ltd.

facility_notes.washrooms: There are several pit toilets available throughout the park.
facility_notes.lunch_space: The main day-use area at Stoltz Pool includes a picnicking area with tables, parking, pit toilets, an information shelter and an all-purpose playing field. The picnic area overlooks the river from a grassy area nestled in a grove of large maple trees.
facility_notes.wheelchair_accessible: Accessibility information is available for these areas of the park: Holt Creek, Horseshoe Bend Group Use Area, Marie Canyon, Skutz Falls, Stoltz Pool, Trestle 66.
facility_notes.bus_parking: The road in to the Horseshoe Bend group campsite is narrow and bumpy and not recommended for large RVs or trailers. Parking is in a gravel lot above the site, and past the parking lot there is no turnaround.

restrictions: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash and under control all times.
Bicycles must keep to roadways or the Trans Canada Trail. Bicycles are not permitted on developed hiking trails.
Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia.
Bicycles with electric assist motors are not allowed on the trails within Cowichan River Park and are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted.
There are no lifeguards on duty in BC Parks.
venue.hours_notes: The park gate is open year-round.
venue.seasonal_notes: Stoltz Pool campground is open all year with a winter camping fee. Its listed operating season is 1 April to 31 October 2026 and reservations run 8 May to 6 September 2026. All fishing is often closed on this section of the river from October to mid December.
venue.price_year_or_season: 2026 camping season, with a winter rate covering 1 November 2025 to 31 March 2026

programs.name: Youth group camping
programs.description: BC Parks offers a reduced youth group camping rate at the two group campsites in this park, Stoltz Pool and Horseshoe Bend. It costs $1 a person a night for a party of at least 12 people, with a minimum charge of $50 a night and a maximum of $150 a night. To qualify, the group has to be attached to a school, a recreation centre or a non profit youth organisation in British Columbia. The party needs at least one adult for every eight children and no more than one adult for every four. Stoltz Pool group site has 12 tent pads, two pit toilets, an open air shelter that fits four picnic tables and a fire pit. Horseshoe Bend sits beside the river among the trees with 11 tent pads and a shelter with a wood stove and picnic tables inside and out. Booking is through the BC Parks reservation service and can be made up to 12 months ahead. There is a boil water notice on the pumped water in this park.
programs.what_children_do: Camp beside the Cowichan River in tents on prepared pads, cook around a fire pit or under an open shelter, and walk the riverside trails, watch for spawning salmon and swim or paddle at Stoltz Pool.
programs.our_note: The river runs right past the Horseshoe Bend site and BC Parks says outright to watch small children there, and that it can be dangerous in autumn, winter and spring. The health authority also says to boil the pump water before drinking it or brushing teeth, so plan to carry your own or bring a way to boil it.
programs.practical_summary: Pit toilets, picnic tables, fire pits and a shelter at each group site, and drinking water only from hand pumps that have to be boiled first. There is no indoor building, so wet weather has no backup, and the road into Horseshoe Bend is not suited to anything large.
programs.extra_fees_note: The $1 a head is charged for every person, adults included, and there is a floor of $50 and a ceiling of $150 a night. Booking fees are charged on top and are not refundable. Changes and cancellations made through the reservation service cost $6 a site.
programs.payment_timing: You pay all your camping and booking fees when you make the reservation.
programs.cancellation_note: Cancel 28 days or more before you arrive and your camping fees come back. Cancel later than that and they do not. Booking fees are never refunded.

chaperone_ratio.applies_to: youth group camping, at least one adult for every eight youths or children

programs.name: Day visit to the park
programs.description: There are four day use areas at Cowichan River Park. Stoltz Pool is the main one, next to the campground, with a boat launch, a riverside trail, picnic tables, parking, pit toilets, an information shelter and an all purpose playing field, and it is where swimming and canoeing happen. Skutz Falls has parking, pit toilets, picnic tables, a river pull out and an information shelter, and looks onto river rapids and a man made fish ladder. Marie Canyon has parking, pit toilets, an information shelter and a trail down to the canyon bottom. The 66 Mile Trestle area has parking, pit toilets, picnic tables and an information shelter. Trails include a short gentle loop at Stoltz Pool, the 8 km Skutz and 66 Mile loop, and the 20 km Cowichan River Footpath, which BC Parks says takes about 6.5 hours end to end. Spawning salmon can be watched at Marie Canyon and Skutz Falls in the autumn. There is no visitor centre and no guided or interpretive program.
programs.what_children_do: Walk a riverside trail, cross a restored railway trestle high above the water, look down into Marie Canyon, watch for spawning salmon at Skutz Falls in autumn, and eat at a picnic table in the maples at Stoltz Pool. There is an open playing field at Stoltz Pool to run in.
programs.our_note: The short loop at Stoltz Pool is the one to pick with small children. The Cowichan River Footpath is 20 km and takes most of a day, and BC Parks warns about steep drop offs and overhanging bluffs along the river, so it is not a walk to take a big mixed group on without a look first.
programs.practical_summary: Pit toilets and picnic tables at all four day use areas, and parking at each. Nothing here is indoors, so there is no shelter from rain, and the only drinking water is from hand pumps that carry a boil water notice.
programs.evidence: There are four day-use areas at Cowichan River Park

images.alt: A wide view from above of a turquoise river bending through a forested valley, with bare deciduous trees along the banks, evergreen hills behind and cloud in a blue sky.
Fast green water running between rock walls thick with yellow green moss, with conifers growing above the banks on both sides.

gaps: RETRIEVAL NOTE: the BC Parks park page renders most of its content in JavaScript. A plain fetch returns the park description and the trails but leaves out the advisories, the whole camping section with its prices, and the whole facilities section with the toilets, picnic areas and accessibility notes. Everything about prices and facilities in this record was read from the live page in a browser.
The website column in the tracker pointed at www.bcparks.ca/explore/parkpgs/, which is a retired directory path. The park's current page is https://bcparks.ca/cowichan-river-park/.
BC Parks writes the name as Cowichan River Park. Cowichan River Provincial Park is the same place.
Whether a day visit costs anything: the park page lists camping fees but says nothing at all about day use fees, so we have not assumed it is free.

No street address is published. The pin comes from the coordinates in the detailed map link on the park page, which is the centre of a park that runs about 20 km along the river with three separate road accesses at Skutz Falls, the Highway 18 connector and Robertson Road. Check which access point you actually want before setting off.
Age or grade limits: none published for youth group camping. The qualifying rule is about the organisation, not the children's ages.
Largest group the group campsites take: not published on the park page. BC Parks says maximum group sizes vary by park and are shown in the reservation system.
Minimum notice for a group booking: not stated. Bookings can be made up to 12 months ahead, but that is a ceiling and not a required notice period.

Months the group campsites are open: not stated separately. The main campground lists an operating season of 1 April to 31 October 2026 with reservations from 8 May to 6 September 2026, and says it is open year round with a winter fee.
No interpretive, guided or school program of any kind is offered here. There is no visitor centre and no staff led activity on the park page.
Drinking water is from hand pumps and the health authority advises boiling it for at least a minute before drinking, brushing teeth or preparing food that will not be cooked.
Rain shelter: the group campsites have open air shelters and Horseshoe Bend has a wood stove, but there is no indoor building anywhere in the park.
A shooting range operates inside the park at 4295 Robertson Road, and BC Parks says walkers near the Glenora trailhead may hear gunshots during range hours.

The two photographs carry no alt text and no visible credit on the page, so we wrote plain descriptions after looking at them. The file names contain a photographer's name but the site prints no credit line, so we recorded none.
